title: Cat-DPO: Category-Adaptive Safety Alignment
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Average safety scores hide weak harm categories; our per-category method beats all baselines on every category, not just overall.
layout: 1 panel, grouped bars per category, dashed average lines, ellipsis and Overall group at right
description: A single wide grouped bar chart of harmlessness score (y-axis 7.0 to 10.0) across eight harm categories, with sample counts in parentheses on the angled x-axis labels. Each category has four bars: pale green Vanilla DPO, teal SACPO, yellow-orange SafeDPO, and Cat-DPO (ours) in orange with a bold black outline. Bars rise in that order, so the outlined orange bar is usually tallest. Two horizontal dashed lines, orange for Cat-DPO and gray for SafeDPO, mark the averages over the eight categories. A small annotation at the right reads 'avg +0.18'. An ellipsis and a dashed vertical divider lead to an 'Overall (1620)' group at the far right, which is partly cut off. The legend sits across the top. The eye goes first to the outlined orange bars and the dashed average lines.
caption: Aggregate harmlessness hides large per-category gaps. Per-category harmlessness (0--10) on PKU-SafeRLHF [ref] for four methods trained on Alpaca-7B [ref], on the $8$ categories where vanilla DPO scores lowest with the overall average. Dashed lines mark \ours{} (orange) and SafeDPO (gray) averaged over the eight. \ours{} is highest on all eight.
abstract: Aligning large language models with human preferences must balance two competing goals: responding helpfully to legitimate requests and reliably refusing harmful ones. Most preference-based safety alignment methods collapse safety into a single scalar that is applied uniformly to every preference pair. The result is a model that appears safe on average but remains relatively unsafe in a minority of harm categories. We cast safety alignment as a per-category constrained optimization problem and derive Cat-DPO, a direct-preference-optimization algorithm with a separate adaptive safety margin for each harm category. The margin tightens when the model still produces unsafe responses in a category and relaxes once the model catches up, so the training signal tracks each category's current difficulty rather than averaging across a single global rate. Across two LLM backbones and six preference-learning baselines, Cat-DPO improves aggregate helpfulness and harmlessness and compresses per-category safety variance and the best-to-worst gap, offering a drop-in per-category refinement of direct preference safety alignment.
